figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of the carbon-aware recommendation framework. Product text denotes the available item metadata used for embedding and PCF estimation, primarily title and category fields in the reported Amazon run.

Figure 2: λ sensitivity for the Electronics category. Each panel plots NDCG@10 (solid, left axis) and AvgPCF@10 (dashed, right axis) as λ increases from the engagement-only baseline (λ = 0) toward carbononly re-ranking (λ = 1). The shaded green region marks operating points whose NDCG@10 remains within 5% of the λ = 0 baseline.
Figure 15: Few-shot LLM prompt template for PCF estimation.

Figure 6: Distribution of predicted PCF (few-shot) across Carbon Catalogue sectors used in PCF estimation diagnostics. Sectors span a wide range, including a heavy industrial tail that drives large errors on the full 866-item holdout relative to the consumer-scale benchmark in Table 1.

Figure 7: Highest-average-PCF categories in the Carbon Catalogue based on the predicted values. A few heavy industrial sectors dominate the extreme tail, which is precisely why full-holdout RMSE paints a much harsher picture of LLM-based estimation than the consumer-scale subset used as the main benchmark.
Figure 8: λ sensitivity for the Home and Kitchen category, shown in the same format as Figure 2; the shaded green region marks settings within a 5% NDCG@10 drop from the λ = 0 baseline.
Figure 9: λ sensitivity for the Sports and Outdoors category, shown in the same format as Figure 2; the shaded green region marks settings within a 5% NDCG@10 drop from the λ = 0 baseline.

Figure 10: Engagement and carbon Pareto frontiers for Electronics. Each point corresponds to one λ value; faint gray points are evaluated but dominated settings, red points and lines denote Pareto-optimal operating points, and the star marks the engagement-only baseline (λ = 0).
Table 2: RecBole training and evaluation hyperparameters.
Figure 12: Engagement and carbon Pareto frontiers for Sports and Outdoors, shown in the same format as Figure 10, with faint gray points denoting dominated λ settings.

Figure 13: Best Pareto operating point per model and category, subject to at least 10% carbon reduction relative to λ = 0. The left panel reports NDCG@10 at the chosen operating point; the right panel reports the corresponding carbon reduction.
Figure 11: Engagement and carbon Pareto frontiers for Home and Kitchen, shown in the same format as Figure 10, with faint gray points denoting dominated λ settings.
Figure 4: Heatmap of maximum carbon reduction (%) achievable while limiting NDCG@10 degradation to at most 5% relative to the λ = 0 baseline, across all model and category combinations.

Figure 3: Multi-model Pareto frontier comparison. Each panel overlays the Pareto-optimal trade-offs of BPR, LightGCN, and NeuMF for one category; curves closer to the upper-left corner offer a better engagement and carbon trade-off. Faint points show evaluated λ settings that are dominated, while the darker connected points show the Pareto-optimal subset.

Figure 14: Cross-category Pareto frontier comparison, one panel per model. Each panel overlays the three product categories to isolate category effects while holding the recommendation backbone fixed.

Figure 5: PCF estimation accuracy on the full 866-item holdout and the consumer-scale subset (PCFtrue ≤ 10,000). The full-holdout error metrics are dominated by a small number of extreme industrial products, whereas the consumer-scale subset is better aligned with the Amazon recommendation setting studied downstream.
